title: Integrity: lock files, SBOMs, signatures and SRI
summary: Make sure what you build and serve is what you meant: locked dependency versions, package source mapping against dependency confusion, an SBOM per release, signed artifacts, and Subresource Integrity for scripts from a CDN.

steps.title: How the supply chain gets attacked
body: **A03:2025 Software Supply Chain Failures** and **A08 Software or Data Integrity Failures** cover attacks on everything between a developer's keyboard and production:
- **Typosquatting**: `Newtonsoft.Jsom`, `reqeusts`: a malicious package one typo away.
- **Dependency confusion**: your internal package `Shop.Payments` is also published, with a higher version, on the public feed, and the build picks the public one.
- **Compromised maintainers or packages**: a real package's new version ships malware (the 2024 `xz` backdoor; npm worms that steal tokens and publish themselves).
- **Compromised build**: the CI system or a build action is changed to inject code (SolarWinds, 2020).
- **Changed CDN files**: a script loaded from a third-party CDN is replaced (the 2024 polyfill.io takeover served malicious code to more than 100,000 sites).
Each has a control: pin and lock versions, map package sources, review new dependencies, sign and verify artifacts, and check hashes of what you load.

steps.prompt: Match each attack to the control that stops it.
pairs: A new transitive version appears between two builds
A CDN serves a changed script
A tampered container image is deployed
"Which of our apps contain this vulnerable library?"

steps.title: The controls, in .NET terms
body: <!-- Directory.Build.props: lock the whole graph, and fail if it would change in CI -->
<!-- nuget.config: each package comes from exactly one feed -->

- **SBOM** (software bill of materials): a machine-readable list of every component and version in a release, in **CycloneDX** or **SPDX** format (`dotnet CycloneDX Shop.sln -o sbom`, or Microsoft's `sbom-tool`). When the next big advisory lands, you search SBOMs instead of guessing.

- **Signing**: NuGet packages can be author- and repository-signed (`<trustedSigners>` in nuget.config); container images and other artifacts are signed with **Sigstore cosign**, and **SLSA provenance** records which build produced which artifact from which commit.

- **SRI** for anything loaded from someone else's server: `<script src="https://cdn.example/lib.js" integrity="sha384-..." crossorigin="anonymous">`. The browser refuses the file if its hash differs. Better still, serve it yourself.

steps.prompt: Your build uses the internal package `Shop.Payments` (a floating version, `*`) from the company feed, and also has nuget.org configured, without source mapping. Someone publishes `Shop.Payments` 9.0.0 on nuget.org. What protects you?
options: Package source mapping (Shop.* only from the internal feed) and exact, locked versions
Nothing is needed: NuGet always prefers the first feed
Signing your own packages, without checking signatures
A WAF in front of the build agents
steps.explain: Without mapping, NuGet considers every feed and takes the best match, which for a floating version is the highest. Mapping pins where each package may come from; exact versions and a lock file pin which one.

steps.prompt: What does this print? (The SRI value is the algorithm, a dash, and the Base64 of the hash.)
steps.explain: SHA-384 gives 48 bytes. Any change to the file gives a different hash, and the browser refuses it.

steps.title: Check a vendored script against its SRI
prompt: The build checks every script it copies from a CDN against the `integrity` value in the page. Write `bool MatchesIntegrity(byte[] content, string integrity)` (`using System.Security.Cryptography;`):
- `integrity` is one or more space-separated tokens `alg-Base64`, where `alg` is `sha256`, `sha384` or `sha512`; tokens may have options after a `?` (ignore them);
- like a browser, use only the tokens of the **strongest** algorithm present (sha512 > sha384 > sha256), and match if **any** of those equals the hash of `content`;
- unknown algorithms are ignored; no usable token, or bad Base64, means `false`. Compare hashes in constant time.
starter: bool MatchesIntegrity(byte[] content, string integrity) => true;
solution: var actual = best switch { 1 => SHA256.HashData(content), 2 => SHA384.HashData(content), _ => SHA512.HashData(content) };
foreach (var t in tokens.Where(t => t.Rank == best))
hints: Split on spaces, drop anything after `?`, split each token at the first `-` into algorithm and value.
Rank the algorithms (sha256 1, sha384 2, sha512 3), keep only the highest rank, hash `content` with that algorithm and compare to each value.
template: string S(string alg, byte[] b) => alg + "-" + Convert.ToBase64String(alg switch { "sha256" => SHA256.HashData(b), "sha384" => SHA384.HashData(b), _ => SHA512.HashData(b) });
Dojo.Eq("the right sha384 matches", true, MatchesIntegrity(lib, S("sha384", lib)));
Dojo.Eq("a changed file does not", false, MatchesIntegrity(evil, S("sha384", lib)));
Dojo.Eq("any of several strongest tokens may match", true, MatchesIntegrity(lib, S("sha512", evil) + " " + S("sha512", lib)));
Dojo.Eq("only the strongest algorithm counts", false, MatchesIntegrity(lib, S("sha256", lib) + " " + S("sha512", evil)));
Dojo.Eq("options after ? are ignored", true, MatchesIntegrity(lib, S("sha256", lib) + "?ct=application/javascript"));
Dojo.Eq("unknown algorithms are ignored", true, MatchesIntegrity(lib, "md5-AAAA " + S("sha256", lib)));
Dojo.Eq("only unknown algorithms: false", false, MatchesIntegrity(lib, "md5-AAAA sha1-BBBB"));
Dojo.Eq("bad Base64: false, not a crash", false, MatchesIntegrity(lib, "sha384-!!!"));
